title: Favorite trumpeters: Keppard, Bunk, and sweet versus straight styles
summary: He recalls hearing Oliver talk, Freddie Keppard and Bunk Johnson at the Entertainers, and contrasts sweet players like Metoyer with Perez.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Where they had the dances near there too. We've got a few more minutes on here. Who were your favorite trumpet players? You mentioned you like Manuel Perez and a few others.
Manuel Perez. Joe, wasn't Joe? Joe Nicklaus.
Did you hear Joe Oliver when you were a kid?
I heard a lot of talk of Joe Oliver. I mean, being young, I just remember, you know.
Very young. But Freddie Kepard, I guess, left town pretty early.
No, I heard Freddie Kepard.
How did you like him?
Oh, he was a fine trumpet player. I also heard Bunk before he...
In the old days.
In the old days, yeah. Before he made his second comeback.
What was he like, Bunk? Bunk? Was he the same as he did later?
I think so. To my idea, he did, yeah.
Who did he play with when you heard him? Was it in the country or right here in the city?

No, in the city. It was a colored nightclub. They called the Entertainers. Anormatwai was working there. He used to go there and wrestle Anormatwai after, you know, he gets off a job here. And everybody would be hollering for him. Bunk, play a number. Play a number, Bunk. But you know he always liked the juice. He had to get his juice voice before he'd get up there. And Anormatwai was another fine trumpet player but he was a different type. He was a sweet type, you know. Sweet, straight, solo.
What would happen when Anormatwai or Perez or that school would have to play a blues? How would they do?

Well Anormatwai could play a blues but they were sweet and soft. It was, you know, more people used to call him a Paula trumpet player. But he could play sweet and soft. He wasn't a flashy trumpet player.
Would he play variations?
Yeah, he would play variations.
Now what would Perez do if he had to play a blues?
Well, Perez would play a straight out blues. Just straight out. There was nothing extra to it. I mean, whatever he played is just like a person who read a poem, you know. It was just straight out.
Would he pick a number like, say, St. Louis Blues or would he just make the blues in B-flat or just anything like that?

Well, B-flat blues or St. Louis Blues. Do you know what I mean? He wouldn't put nothing extra to it. No more than what it'd go. Of course, the average trumpet player or musician, whenever they play a number like that and they would be too far in between, you know, slack in between, they always make some kind of variation to fill in. But he wouldn't. It would be up to somebody else in the band to make that.
